supplemental_notices.text:
/*
 *  Javascript porting of Markus Kuhn's wcwidth() implementation
 *
 *  The following explanation comes from the original C implementation:
 *
 *  This is an implementation of wcwidth() and wcswidth() (defined in
 *  IEEE Std 1002.1-2001) for Unicode.
 *
 *  http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcwidth.html
 *  http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcswidth.html
 *
 *  In fixed-width output devices, Latin characters all occupy a single
 *  "cell" position of equal width, whereas ideographic CJK characters
 *  occupy two such cells. Interoperability between terminal-line
 *  applications and (teletype-style) character terminals using the
 *  UTF-8 encoding requires agreement on which character should advance
 *  the cursor by how many cell positions. No established formal
 *  standards exist at present on which Unicode character shall occupy
 *  how many cell positions on character terminals. These routines are
 *  a first attempt of defining such behavior based on simple rules
 *  applied to data provided by the Unicode Consortium.
 *
 *  For some graphical characters, the Unicode standard explicitly
 *  defines a character-cell width via the definition of the East Asian
 *  FullWidth (F), Wide (W), Half-width (H), and Narrow (Na) classes.
 *  In all these cases, there is no ambiguity about which width a
 *  terminal shall use. For characters in the East Asian Ambiguous (A)
 *  class, the width choice depends purely on a preference of backward
 *  compatibility with either historic CJK or Western practice.
 *  Choosing single-width for these characters is easy to justify as
 *  the appropriate long-term solution, as the CJK practice of
 *  displaying these characters as double-width comes from historic
 *  implementation simplicity (8-bit encoded characters were displayed
 *  single-width and 16-bit ones double-width, even for Greek,
 *  Cyrillic, etc.) and not any typographic considerations.
 *
 *  Much less clear is the choice of width for the Not East Asian
 *  (Neutral) class. Existing practice does not dictate a width for any
 *  of these characters. It would nevertheless make sense
 *  typographically to allocate two character cells to characters such
 *  as for instance EM SPACE or VOLUME INTEGRAL, which cannot be
 *  represented adequately with a single-width glyph. The following
 *  routines at present merely assign a single-cell width to all
 *  neutral characters, in the interest of simplicity. This is not
 *  entirely satisfactory and should be reconsidered before
 *  establishing a formal standard in this area. At the moment, the
 *  decision which Not East Asian (Neutral) characters should be
 *  represented by double-width glyphs cannot yet be answered by
 *  applying a simple rule from the Unicode database content. Setting
 *  up a proper standard for the behavior of UTF-8 character terminals
 *  will require a careful analysis not only of each Unicode character,
 *  but also of each presentation form, something the author of these
 *  routines has avoided to do so far.

 *  Latest version: http://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mgk25/ucs/wcwidth.c

 * http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcswidth.html
 *
 * In fixed-width output devices, Latin characters all occupy a single
 * "cell" position of equal width, whereas ideographic CJK characters
 * occupy two such cells. Interoperability between terminal-line
 * applications and (teletype-style) character terminals using the
 * UTF-8 encoding requires agreement on which character should advance
 * the cursor by how many cell positions. No established formal
 * standards exist at present on which Unicode character shall occupy
 * how many cell positions on character terminals. These routines are

 * applied to data provided by the Unicode Consortium.

 * defines a character-cell width via the definition of the East Asian
 * FullWidth (F), Wide (W), Half-width (H), and Narrow (Na) classes.
 * In all these cases, there is no ambiguity about which width a
 * terminal shall use. For characters in the East Asian Ambiguous (A)
 * class, the width choice depends purely on a preference of backward
 * compatibility with either historic CJK or Western practice.
 * Choosing single-width for these characters is easy to justify as
 * the appropriate long-term solution, as the CJK practice of
 * displaying these characters as double-width comes from historic
 * implementation simplicity (8-bit encoded characters were displayed
 * single-width and 16-bit ones double-width, even for Greek,
 * Cyrillic, etc.) and not any typographic considerations.
 *
 * Much less clear is the choice of width for the Not East Asian
 * (Neutral) class. Existing practice does not dictate a width for any
 * of these characters. It would nevertheless make sense
 * typographically to allocate two character cells to characters such
 * as for instance EM SPACE or VOLUME INTEGRAL, which cannot be
 * represented adequately with a single-width glyph. The following
 * routines at present merely assign a single-cell width to all
 * neutral characters, in the interest of simplicity. This is not
 * entirely satisfactory and should be reconsidered before
 * establishing a formal standard in this area. At the moment, the
 * decision which Not East Asian (Neutral) characters should be
 * represented by double-width glyphs cannot yet be answered by

 * will require a careful analysis not only of each Unicode character,
 * but also of each presentation form, something the author of these
 * routines has avoided to do so far.
 *
 * http://www.unicode.org/unicode/reports/tr11/
 *

sections.interpretation_and_version_applicability: The initial 2012 port explicitly identifies Kuhn’s C implementation, embeds its dated 2007-05-26 Unicode 5.0 attribution and complete no-fee use/copy/modify/distribute grant and warranty disclaimer. Its LICENSE and README independently identify the same source. The recorded comparison makes this commit an ancestor of the npm gitHead, and all 142 ordered combining ranges match the exact published 2.0.0 package and the retained author C source. This supports applying the embedded historical grant to the identified incorporated upstream material; the port retains its own exact published terms. The author C URL response is not itself an immutable historical revision, and ancestry and matching tables do not prove every intervening byte or source provenance of every component.
sections.obligations: Retain the complete published port copyright and permission notice in copies or substantial portions and preserve its disclaimer. The embedded upstream grant states no express notice-retention condition; preserve its complete attribution, grant and disclaimer as supplemental evidence.

source_evidence.behavioral_inspection: The port LICENSE, README, and index explicitly attribute a port of Kuhn wcwidth; README links the same author URL. Binary-search structure, control checks and wide-character thresholds correspond closely to the C. The C source says Unicode 5.0 dated 2007-05-26; the JS files do not assert a Unicode version, although the table matches. JS defaults control to 0, permits configurable nul/control, decodes UTF-16 surrogate pairs and accepts numeric input; C returns -1 for controls and its bounded wchar string loop stops at NUL. C also includes CJK ambiguous-width variants absent in the port. These are inspection findings, not executed semantic equivalence tests.

supplemental_notices.text:
/*
 *  Javascript porting of Markus Kuhn's wcwidth() implementation
 *
 *  The following explanation comes from the original C implementation:
 *
 *  This is an implementation of wcwidth() and wcswidth() (defined in
 *  IEEE Std 1002.1-2001) for Unicode.
 *
 *  http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcwidth.html
 *  http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcswidth.html
 *
 *  In fixed-width output devices, Latin characters all occupy a single
 *  "cell" position of equal width, whereas ideographic CJK characters
 *  occupy two such cells. Interoperability between terminal-line
 *  applications and (teletype-style) character terminals using the
 *  UTF-8 encoding requires agreement on which character should advance
 *  the cursor by how many cell positions. No established formal
 *  standards exist at present on which Unicode character shall occupy
 *  how many cell positions on character terminals. These routines are
 *  a first attempt of defining such behavior based on simple rules
 *  applied to data provided by the Unicode Consortium.
 *
 *  For some graphical characters, the Unicode standard explicitly
 *  defines a character-cell width via the definition of the East Asian
 *  FullWidth (F), Wide (W), Half-width (H), and Narrow (Na) classes.
 *  In all these cases, there is no ambiguity about which width a
 *  terminal shall use. For characters in the East Asian Ambiguous (A)
 *  class, the width choice depends purely on a preference of backward
 *  compatibility with either historic CJK or Western practice.
 *  Choosing single-width for these characters is easy to justify as
 *  the appropriate long-term solution, as the CJK practice of
 *  displaying these characters as double-width comes from historic
 *  implementation simplicity (8-bit encoded characters were displayed
 *  single-width and 16-bit ones double-width, even for Greek,
 *  Cyrillic, etc.) and not any typographic considerations.
 *
 *  Much less clear is the choice of width for the Not East Asian
 *  (Neutral) class. Existing practice does not dictate a width for any
 *  of these characters. It would nevertheless make sense
 *  typographically to allocate two character cells to characters such
 *  as for instance EM SPACE or VOLUME INTEGRAL, which cannot be
 *  represented adequately with a single-width glyph. The following
 *  routines at present merely assign a single-cell width to all
 *  neutral characters, in the interest of simplicity. This is not
 *  entirely satisfactory and should be reconsidered before
 *  establishing a formal standard in this area. At the moment, the
 *  decision which Not East Asian (Neutral) characters should be
 *  represented by double-width glyphs cannot yet be answered by
 *  applying a simple rule from the Unicode database content. Setting
 *  up a proper standard for the behavior of UTF-8 character terminals
 *  will require a careful analysis not only of each Unicode character,
 *  but also of each presentation form, something the author of these
 *  routines has avoided to do so far.
 *
 *  http://www.unicode.org/unicode/reports/tr11/
 *
 *  Markus Kuhn -- 2007-05-26 (Unicode 5.0)
 *
 *  Permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute this software
 *  for any purpose and without fee is hereby granted. The author
 *  disclaims all warranties with regard to this software.
 *
 *  Latest version: http://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mgk25/ucs/wcwidth.c
 */

 * http://www.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007904975/functions/wcswidth.html
 *

 * UTF-8 encoding requires agreement on which character should advance
 * the cursor by how many cell positions. No established formal
 * standards exist at present on which Unicode character shall occupy
 * how many cell positions on character terminals. These routines are
 * a first attempt of defining such behavior based on simple rules
 * applied to data provided by the Unicode Consortium.
 *
 * For some graphical characters, the Unicode standard explicitly
 * defines a character-cell width via the definition of the East Asian
 * FullWidth (F), Wide (W), Half-width (H), and Narrow (Na) classes.
 * In all these cases, there is no ambiguity about which width a
 * terminal shall use. For characters in the East Asian Ambiguous (A)
 * class, the width choice depends purely on a preference of backward
 * compatibility with either historic CJK or Western practice.
 * Choosing single-width for these characters is easy to justify as
 * the appropriate long-term solution, as the CJK practice of
 * displaying these characters as double-width comes from historic
 * implementation simplicity (8-bit encoded characters were displayed
 * single-width and 16-bit ones double-width, even for Greek,
 * Cyrillic, etc.) and not any typographic considerations.
 *
 * Much less clear is the choice of width for the Not East Asian
 * (Neutral) class. Existing practice does not dictate a width for any
 * of these characters. It would nevertheless make sense
 * typographically to allocate two character cells to characters such
 * as for instance EM SPACE or VOLUME INTEGRAL, which cannot be
 * represented adequately with a single-width glyph. The following
 * routines at present merely assign a single-cell width to all
 * neutral characters, in the interest of simplicity. This is not
 * entirely satisfactory and should be reconsidered before
 * establishing a formal standard in this area. At the moment, the
 * decision which Not East Asian (Neutral) characters should be
 * represented by double-width glyphs cannot yet be answered by
 * applying a simple rule from the Unicode database content. Setting
 * up a proper standard for the behavior of UTF-8 character terminals
 * will require a careful analysis not only of each Unicode character,
 * but also of each presentation form, something the author of these
 * routines has avoided to do so far.
 *
 * http://www.unicode.org/unicode/reports/tr11/
 *
 * Markus Kuhn -- 2007-05-26 (Unicode 5.0)
 *
 * Permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute this software
 * for any purpose and without fee is hereby granted. The author
 * disclaims all warranties with regard to this software.
 *
 * Latest version: http://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mgk25/ucs/wcwidth.c
 */

supplemental_decision.interpretation_and_version_applicability: The initial 2012 port explicitly identifies Kuhn’s C implementation, embeds its dated 2007-05-26 Unicode 5.0 attribution and complete no-fee use/copy/modify/distribute grant and warranty disclaimer. Its LICENSE and README independently identify the same source. The recorded comparison makes this commit an ancestor of the npm gitHead, and all 142 ordered combining ranges match the exact published 2.0.0 package and the retained author C source. This supports applying the embedded historical grant to the identified incorporated upstream material; the port retains its own exact published terms. The author C URL response is not itself an immutable historical revision, and ancestry and matching tables do not prove every intervening byte or source provenance of every component.
supplemental_decision.obligations: Retain the complete published port copyright and permission notice in copies or substantial portions and preserve its disclaimer. The embedded upstream grant states no express notice-retention condition; preserve its complete attribution, grant and disclaimer as supplemental evidence.

source_evidence.behavioral_inspection: The port LICENSE, README, and index explicitly attribute a port of Kuhn wcwidth; README links the same author URL. Binary-search structure, control checks and wide-character thresholds correspond closely to the C. The C source says Unicode 5.0 dated 2007-05-26; the JS files do not assert a Unicode version, although the table matches. JS defaults control to 0, permits configurable nul/control, decodes UTF-16 surrogate pairs and accepts numeric input; C returns -1 for controls and its bounded wchar string loop stops at NUL. C also includes CJK ambiguous-width variants absent in the port. These are inspection findings, not executed semantic equivalence tests.
